title: Business Continuity, HA, and Disaster Recovery: RPO, RTO, and Cost Trade-offs
bodyMarkdown:
## High availability versus disaster recovery

These solve different problems and the exam punishes mixing them up.

- **High availability (HA)** keeps a service running through *component* failures such as a VM, a disk or a whole zone. It is built from redundancy inside one deployment and relies on automation, not people.
- **Disaster recovery (DR)** restores a service after a *large-scale* failure: loss of a region, corruption, deletion, ransomware, a bad deploy of data. It relies on copies in another failure domain plus a tested recovery procedure.

A design can have excellent HA and no DR at all. A Cloud SQL instance with HA enabled survives a zone failure and still loses everything that was in the region if the region goes away, and it also faithfully replicates an accidental `DELETE` to its standby. HA is not a backup.

## RPO and RTO

| Metric | Meaning | Answers |
|--------|---------|---------|
| **RPO** (recovery point objective) | Maximum acceptable *data loss*, measured as time | How far back can the recovered data be? |
| **RTO** (recovery time objective) | Maximum acceptable *downtime* | How long until service is back? |

The [DR planning guide](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/dr-scenarios-planning-guide) defines RTO as how long an application can stay offline after a major incident and RPO as how much data loss is tolerable, and notes the smaller your RTO and RPO, the more the application costs to run. Two practical rules follow:

- **RPO is set by how data is copied, not by how fast you restore.** A nightly export gives an RPO of up to about 24 hours no matter how quick the restore is, so it cannot satisfy a 5-minute RPO. Tight RPOs need continuous protection: synchronous replication, point-in-time recovery or streaming replication.
- **RTO is set by how much of the recovery is automated.** The DR guide's own framing is that an RTO measured in minutes means designing an application that recovers automatically without human intervention. If recovery needs someone to run a script, plan for a longer RTO.

The same guide explains the replication trade-off: synchronous replication means you do not lose data during an infrastructure outage but adds latency, while asynchronous replication gives lower latency and higher throughput at the expense of data protection. Synchronous cross-region designs are therefore only sensible where the write-latency cost is acceptable.

## DR strategy spectrum

| Pattern | What is running at the DR site | Recovery behavior | Relative cost | Fits |
|---------|-------------------------------|-------------------|---------------|------|
| **Backup and restore** (cold) | Nothing; only copies of data and templates | Provision infrastructure, then restore data; longest RTO, RPO equals the backup interval | Lowest | Tier 3, tolerant workloads |
| **Pilot light / warm standby** | Data replicated; minimal or scaled-down compute | Scale up and switch traffic; shorter RTO, RPO equals replication lag | Medium | Tier 2, important workloads |
| **Hot / active-active** | Full capacity serving traffic in two or more locations | Automatic traffic shift; near-zero RTO, RPO near zero when replication is synchronous | Highest | Tier 1, revenue-critical |

Tier the portfolio. The exam repeatedly describes one company with a critical transactional system and a tolerant reporting system, and the correct answer applies a different pattern to each. Paying for active-active on the reporting database fails the cost pillar; running the payments database on a single region with nightly backups fails reliability.

The Well-Architected [reliability pillar](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability) adds two testing principles that are easy to forget: perform testing for recovery from failures, and perform testing for recovery from data loss. A restore that has never been exercised is an assumption, not a plan. Automate provisioning of the recovery environment with infrastructure as code so RTO does not depend on someone's memory.

## HA building blocks on Google Cloud

**Compute.** A [regional managed instance group](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/regional-migs) spreads VMs across zones. The default is three zones, you can pick fewer, or more than three by listing zones explicitly. The default distribution shape is EVEN, which keeps the same VM count in each selected zone. The detail that matters for capacity planning: when a zone fails, the instances in the remaining zones keep serving, but no new instances are added and none are redistributed unless autoscaling is configured. Two consequences:

- Enable autoscaling so lost capacity is replaced in surviving zones.
- Over-provision for zone loss. With three zones and the load split evenly, each zone carries one third; after losing one, the other two must each carry half, so you need roughly 50% headroom over steady-state demand to avoid saturation during the event.

[Autohealing](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/autohealing-instances-in-migs) needs a health check; a VM whose application stops responding is marked unhealthy and recreated. Google recommends a separate, more conservative health check for autohealing than for load balancing (for example a low healthy threshold such as 1 and a higher unhealthy threshold such as 3) so a brief blip does not trigger recreation. Use an application-level check, not just VM status.

**Load balancing.** The [load balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview) separates global external Application Load Balancers, which expose a single anycast IP and can front backends in multiple regions, from regional external ones, which are limited to one region. For worldwide users with automatic routing to the nearest healthy backend, the global external Application Load Balancer is the building block, and [Cloud CDN](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/overview) integrates with it to serve cacheable content from Google's edge. Note that CDN caches fill reactively on client requests rather than being pre-replicated between caches.

**Databases and their failure domains.**

| Service and configuration | Survives | Does not survive | Notes |
|---------------------------|----------|------------------|-------|
| Cloud SQL with HA | Loss of the primary's zone; automatic failover | Loss of the region; logical errors | Primary and standby in two zones with synchronous replication to each zone's persistent disk; failover takes roughly 60 seconds per the [HA documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability); HA doubles instance cost |
| Cloud SQL cross-region replica | Regional outage, after manual promotion | Instant, automatic recovery | The docs describe promoting replicas manually for regional failure |
| Spanner regional | Zone failure | Region failure | 99.99% availability SLA, three read-write replicas across zones |
| Spanner dual-region or multi-region | Region failure | n/a | 99.999% SLA, [replicas across regions](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) with a witness in a third region for multi-region |
| Cloud Storage regional | Zone loss | Region loss | Data stored redundantly across at least two zones |
| Cloud Storage dual or multi-region | Region loss | Instant cross-region RPO | Cross-region replication is asynchronous |

The [Cloud Storage availability and durability](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/availability-durability) page spells out the RPO of that asynchronous replication: default replication is designed to cover 99.9% of newly written objects within one hour and 100% within 12 hours, while turbo replication (dual-region buckets only) targets a 15-minute RPO. So a multi-region bucket is not a zero-RPO design, which matters when a question pairs object storage with a strict RPO.

## Backup and recovery essentials

- **Point-in-time recovery (PITR).** For Cloud SQL MySQL it uses binary logs plus backups, requires binary logging and backups to be enabled, and always [restores to a new instance](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/pitr), never in place. It answers "undo yesterday's bad write", which replication cannot.
- **Disk snapshots.** [Standard snapshots](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/snapshots) are incremental (the first is full, later ones hold changed blocks) and stored across multiple locations; archive snapshots are cheaper for compliance and long-term retention; instant snapshots are local to the zone or region and disappear with the source disk, so they are not DR copies. Deleted standard snapshots are retained for three days. Schedule snapshots rather than relying on manual runs.
- **Backup and DR Service.** [Backup and DR](https://cloud.google.com/backup-disaster-recovery/docs/concepts/backup-dr) provides centrally managed, application-consistent backups for Compute Engine VMs, Persistent Disk, Filestore, VMware Engine, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and self-managed databases such as Oracle, SQL Server and SAP HANA. Backup vaults enforce write-once-read-many immutability with retention up to 99 years, which is the answer for ransomware-resistant, tamper-proof copies. The legacy management console is being phased out; the docs state support for new backups there ends September 30, 2027.
- **Cloud Storage object versioning and retention** protect against overwrite and deletion within a bucket, but not against loss of the location.

## Worked example

A healthcare platform needs patient-record writes to survive a regional outage with near-zero RPO, while reporting can tolerate hours of downtime and data loss.

- Critical database: Spanner multi-region. Replication across regions is built in, no failover scripting is needed, and the SLA is 99.999%.
- Web tier: regional or global external Application Load Balancer in front of regional MIGs with autohealing, autoscaling and zone-loss headroom.
- Reporting database: Cloud SQL with scheduled backups and a cross-region copy, or restore from backups into a new region when needed. Cheaper, and the long RTO is accepted.
- Ransomware or operator error: Backup and DR vault with immutability, because replication would copy the damage.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Calling HA a DR plan.** HA protects against component and zone failures; it does not protect against regional loss or logical corruption.
- **Ignoring the backup interval.** An RPO tighter than the backup frequency is not met by that backup.
- **Zonal "high availability".** A single-zone MIG with autoscaling or a lone VM with snapshots loses everything when the zone goes.
- **Same-region copies for regional DR.** Instant snapshots and regional buckets are in the failure domain you are trying to escape.
- **Uniform active-active.** Applying tier-1 patterns to every workload burns budget.
- **Unmanaged manual failover for tight RTOs.** Two unmanaged instances with a hand-edited DNS record cannot deliver an RTO of minutes.
- **Never testing restores or failover,** or storing runbooks in the system that is down.
- **Forgetting capacity after failover.** The surviving zone or region must absorb the load, and quota there must be available.

## Exam tips

- **HA and DR are different.** Zone failure means regional MIG, regional or HA database, load balancer; region failure means data and compute in another region.
- **Compare the backup interval to the RPO first.** A nightly backup fails a 5-minute RPO; the right fix is continuous replication or PITR, not a faster restore.
- **Tier the answer.** When a scenario mixes critical and tolerant workloads, pick Spanner multi-region or active-active for the critical part and backup and restore or warm standby for the rest.
- **Regional MIG plus autohealing plus autoscaling plus load balancer** is the standard no-manual-intervention answer for stateless zone survival; unmanaged instances and manual DNS are distractors.
- **Cloud SQL HA is zonal protection with roughly one minute of failover;** cross-region replicas need manual promotion, and PITR always creates a new instance.
- **Know the Spanner SLAs:** 99.99% regional, 99.999% for dual-region and multi-region configurations.
- **Global external Application Load Balancer plus Cloud CDN** is the pattern for worldwide users needing a single anycast entry point and nearest-healthy-backend routing.
- **Immutable, vault-based backups answer ransomware and tamper-resistance questions;** replication and instant snapshots do not.
